Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette:
María is a 19-year-old Latina woman who works as a train conductor, a job she took right out of high school because it offered steady hours and a clear path forward. She lives alone in a small apartment in a quiet part of the city, and she comes to therapy at the urging of her supervisor, who noticed she had been missing shifts and seemed increasingly jumpy on the job. What emerges over the first few sessions is a childhood trauma that has shaped her entire sense of safety and self: when she was seven years old, she witnessed her father beat her mother in their darkened living room. María had been standing in the doorway, frozen, as her mother screamed and her father’s fists landed. She remembers the taste of the cheap red wine her father had been drinking—sour and metallic—because it splashed onto her lips when he knocked over a glass. That taste still returns to her unexpectedly, vivid and unwelcome, and when it does, the memory feels like it is happening right now, not like something from twelve years ago. She cannot put the events of that night in the right order; the images come in fragments—her mother’s face, the sound of a lamp breaking, the dark—and she is never sure what came first.

The darkness is the worst trigger. When she steps into a dark room, or when the train she is driving passes through a tunnel, her heart starts racing, and that pounding in her chest immediately pulls her back into the memory. She has come to believe that she cannot stop bad things from happening to her, and that she failed to protect her mother that night because of the way she acted—or rather, did not act. She was just a child, but that does not matter to the feeling: she should have done something, and her helplessness proves she is fundamentally weak. These appraisals are strongest when a trigger hits; the loud noise of a train horn or a sudden shout in the station makes her heart pound, and in that moment she is certain that she is about to fail again, that something terrible is coming and she will be powerless to stop it.

To cope, María has developed a set of strategies that she relies on daily. She keeps herself busy constantly—working double shifts, cleaning her apartment at odd hours, scrolling through her phone—because when she is still, the memories rush in. She also restricts her eating, skipping meals or eating very little, because she has noticed that hunger keeps her mind sharp and focused on the present, away from the past. And she finds herself thinking, over and over, about how different her life would have been if she had yelled or run for help that night; these counterfactual thoughts are exhausting but feel necessary, as if she might find an answer that finally lets her stop blaming herself.

Her sense of threat is pervasive. At night, she finds it harder to feel safe than during the day, so she checks the locks on her door and windows repeatedly before she can even try to sleep. She is on high alert whenever she hears unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring, a door slamming—and that hypervigilance itself becomes a trigger: the alarm in her body tells her something is wrong, which makes her heart race, which plunges her back into the memory. The more she scans for danger, the more she finds it, and the more she finds it, the more she believes she is helpless and that she failed. She has started avoiding the evening shift at work because the darkness of the tunnels and the night sky feel unbearable, and she has begun calling in sick on days when she knows she will be working late.

These strategies, however, only deepen the cycle. Keeping busy prevents her from processing the memory, so it stays disjointed and present-tense. Undereating leaves her tired and irritable, which makes her feel even more out of control, reinforcing her belief that she cannot protect herself or anyone else. And the counterfactual thinking keeps her stuck in a past she cannot change, feeding her self-blame. The more she avoids the triggers, the more they seem to multiply: a dark hallway at work now makes her heart pound, and that pounding immediately brings the taste of wine back to her mouth, and she is seven years old again, frozen in the doorway.

What finally brought María to therapy was a moment on the train last week. She was driving through a tunnel when a passenger dropped a metal water bottle; the clatter was sharp and sudden. Her heart exploded in her chest, she lost her sense of where she was, and she nearly let go of the controls. Her supervisor pulled her off the route and told her she needed help. María is terrified that she will lose her job, but what frightens her most is the feeling that she is still that little girl, standing in the dark, unable to move. She hopes, more than anything, that therapy can help her feel like an adult who has a say in what happens next.
